claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation is governed primarily by synergistic interactions among Al, Cr, and Ti at matrix grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary Al, Cr, and Ti promote selective oxidation and/or internal oxidation.
Selective or internal oxidation at grain boundaries leads to grain-boundary embrittlement.
Concentration thresholds of Al, Cr, and Ti, together with the retained fcc structure, determine protective-scale formation and stability.
Candidate oxide products include Al2O3, Cr2O3, and TiO2.
The starting additively manufactured alloy has a single-phase fcc matrix.
The starting alloy has notable strength and fatigue performance.
The starting alloy has a uniform microstructure.
Oxide stability and protectiveness depend on local composition and phase stability.
Local composition and phase stability are influenced by the retained fcc matrix and additive-manufacturing-induced microstructure.
Samples with greater grain-boundary enrichment of Al, Cr, and Ti will degrade more rapidly during oxidizing exposure than samples with uniform distributions or lower boundary concentrations.
Greater grain-boundary enrichment will produce increased loss of mechanical integrity, embrittlement, and/or oxide-scale spallation.
Internal oxidation and phase destabilization may occur in reducing environments.
Degradation in reducing environments will be less pronounced than in oxidizing environments unless grain-boundary enrichment is present.
A uniform fcc baseline without grain-boundary enrichment will undergo minimal degradation and retain its mechanical properties under the same exposure conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to alloys with a similar fcc matrix and comparable Al, Cr, and Ti concentrations.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to alloys with bcc or intermetallic phase structures or substantially different elemental ratios.
